"I was so tired yesterday, but I can't remember what I did that day anymore." "I know there are good days and bad days, but I don't know what makes the difference." When living with post-stroke fatigue (PSF), you may feel such frustration. This is because fatigue is invisible, and memories tend to become vague.

The theme of this ninth installment is "How to keep a fatigue diary." You don't need to write a formal diary. By briefly recording your activities, rest, and the intensity of your fatigue for the day, you may start to see your own patterns. 1. Why is "recording" useful?

One of the difficult aspects of PSF is that you may experience "fatigue that is disproportionate to the day's activity level," or it may be difficult to recover even after resting. The American Heart Association's scientific statement (Stroke, 2017) also identifies exhaustion that does not improve with rest as a core symptom.

Even if you try to recall such fatigue later, the sequence and degree become blurred. An impression like "I feel like I was generally in bad shape last week" does not tell you on what kind of days or after what kind of activities your fatigue intensified.

When you have a short record at hand, you can look back on it in a way that is closer to the facts rather than just impressions. For example, you might discover your own unique patterns, such as "fatigue intensifies the day after consecutive outings," "I can move relatively well in the morning, but I crash in the afternoon," or "I feel heavy all day after a night of poor sleep."
